title: Act II, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: After the feast Romeo hides in the Capulet orchard. Mercutio and Benvolio call for him; Mercutio mockingly conjures him by Rosaline's body parts. Benvolio says love is blind; they go home.

vocabulary.context:
I conjure thee by Rosaline’s bright eyes,
By her high forehead and her scarlet lip,
By her fine foot, straight leg and quivering thigh
And the demesnes that there adjacent lie,
That in thy likeness thou appear to us!

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “I conjure thee by Rosaline’s bright eyes” slowly and put it in my own words: Mercutio, not knowing Romeo loves Juliet, mockingly conjures Romeo to appear by Rosaline's bright eyes. Next, craft. I notice the mock-magic "conjure," as if he were summoning a spirit. The strongest word is “conjure”: it is a word for raising spirits, making fun of lovesick Romeo. Then, effect. What is Mercutio doing when he calls on Rosaline's eyes? My answer: When Mercutio calls on Rosaline's eyes, he is mockingly conjuring Romeo like a spirit, teasing him as Rosaline's lover; he does not know Romeo has fallen for Juliet, which sets up the seriousness of the balcony scene.
